scenes.visual: Title card 'Climbing the Evidence Ladder' over a mushroom on a mossy log, rain drops falling. COLOUR MAP (both films): mushroom card PURPLE #8a5a9e, oak card GREEN #2e8b4f, deer card BROWN #a0662b, paramecium card TEAL #0e7c86, bacterium card ORANGE #d0701a, archaeon card CRIMSON #b23b4e (the lesson's simulation colours). Each card is a flat cartoon of the organism with its name underneath, on a white card with a thick left edge in its colour. The EVIDENCE LADDER stands at the left edge, four rungs bottom to top: 'eyes', 'microscope', 'cell chemistry', 'DNA'; the current rung glows gold. Domain boxes are labelled 'Bacteria', 'Archaea', 'Eukarya' in that order left to right, charcoal outlines. All cells are cartoons labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: A mushroom stays in one place, like a plant. So why don't scientists call it a plant? The answer depends on your tools.
scenes.visual: A cartoon mushroom on a log beside a cartoon oak sapling. Both sway slightly in the wind; neither walks away. A question card fades in: 'Why not a plant?'
scenes.narration: A mushroom stays in one place, like a plant. So why don't scientists call it a plant? The answer depends on your tools.

scenes.tts: Here are six living things: a mushroom, an oak, a deer, a paramecium, a bacterium and an archaeon. Scientists sort living things with several kinds of evidence. This ladder orders them; it is not a timeline.
scenes.visual: Six cards deal onto a sorting table one at a time as each is named, in the colour map. Then the four-rung evidence ladder rises at the left edge, rung labels appearing bottom to top, with a small tag beside it: 'kinds of evidence (a model, not a timeline)'.
scenes.narration: Here are six living things: a mushroom, an oak, a deer, a paramecium, a bacterium and an archaeon. Scientists sort living things with several kinds of evidence. This ladder orders them; it is not a timeline.

scenes.tts: The bottom rung is your eyes. The mushroom stays put, like the oak, so it sits with the plants. The deer has an animal's body and walks away, so it goes with the animals. The three tiny ones are too small to make out. For a long time, many scientists grouped mushrooms with plants.
scenes.visual: 'eyes' rung glows. An eye icon scans the table. The mushroom card slides next to the oak card under a header 'Plants'; the deer goes under 'Animals'. The paramecium, bacterium and archaeon cards shrink to blurry specks in a pile labelled 'too small to make out'.
scenes.narration: The bottom rung is your eyes. The mushroom stays put, like the oak, so it sits with the plants. The deer has an animal's body and walks away, so it goes with the animals. The three tiny ones are too small to make out. For a long time, many scientists grouped mushrooms with plants.

scenes.tts: Next rung, the light microscope. It answers three questions. Does each cell have a nucleus, the part that holds its DNA? Which cell parts does it have? Does it have one cell or many? A fourth question needs other tests. Does it make its own food, or take food in?
scenes.visual: 'microscope' rung glows. A cartoon microscope lowers over the table; the blurry pile sharpens into three clear cards. Three clue icons appear inside a lens-shaped frame labelled 'microscope': a cell with a dark dot 'nucleus?', a cell with a thick outline and green ovals 'cell parts?', one cell versus a cluster 'one or many?'. A fourth icon, a sun with a leaf versus a mouth 'makes food or takes it in?', appears beside the frame with a small tag 'other tests'.
scenes.narration: Next rung, the light microscope. It answers three questions. Does each cell have a nucleus, the part that holds its DNA? Which cell parts does it have? Does it have one cell or many? A fourth question needs other tests. Does it make its own food, or take food in?

scenes.tts: The first question splits the cards. Four of them have cells with a nucleus. The bacterium and the archaeon have no nucleus, and under the microscope they look alike.
scenes.visual: The 'nucleus?' icon pulses. A line slides down the table: mushroom, oak, deer and paramecium cards move to one side under 'nucleus'; bacterium and archaeon cards move to the other under 'no nucleus'. Their two cartoon cells, side by side, are drawn identical.
scenes.narration: The first question splits the cards. Four of them have cells with a nucleus. The bacterium and the archaeon have no nucleus, and under the microscope they look alike.

scenes.tts: Now zoom in on the mushroom. Its cells have a nucleus and a cell wall, like a plant's. But they have no chloroplasts, the green parts where a cell makes sugar using light.
scenes.visual: Zoom into a cartoon mushroom cell next to a cartoon oak leaf cell, both labelled 'schematic'. Both show a dark nucleus and a thick wall, ticked. The oak cell has green ovals labelled 'chloroplasts'; the mushroom cell has none, and a red empty-circle mark sits where they would be.
scenes.narration: Now zoom in on the mushroom. Its cells have a nucleus and a cell wall, like a plant's. But they have no chloroplasts, the green parts where a cell makes sugar using light.

scenes.tts: So a mushroom cannot make its own food. It releases digesting substances into the log. They break the wood into tiny dissolved pieces, and the mushroom takes them in. Most plants make their own food instead. So the mushroom slides out of the plant group. Later, fungi got a kingdom of their own.
scenes.visual: Inset: fungal threads in the wood release small purple droplets; the wood around them fades into tiny dissolved dots (no solid crumbs); the dots pass into the threads. Then the mushroom card slides away from the oak card into a new box labelled 'Fungi', with a small tag 'later: kingdom Fungi'. The oak stays in 'Plants'.
scenes.narration: So a mushroom cannot make its own food. It releases digesting substances into the log. They break the wood into tiny dissolved pieces, and the mushroom takes them in. Most plants make their own food instead. So the mushroom slides out of the plant group. Later, fungi got a kingdom of their own.

scenes.tts: Third rung, cell chemistry. The bacterium and the archaeon look the same under a microscope. Are they the same kind of living thing?
scenes.visual: 'cell chemistry' rung glows. The bacterium and archaeon cards sit side by side under a magnifier; their cartoon cells look identical. Question card: 'Same kind?'
scenes.narration: Third rung, cell chemistry. The bacterium and the archaeon look the same under a microscope. Are they the same kind of living thing?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card 'Same kind?' holds over the two identical cells; a 5-second ring timer runs at bottom right.

scenes.tts: No. The chemicals that build their cell walls and membranes are different. Their genes, compared on the top rung, differ too. So scientists split them into two domains, Bacteria and Archaea.
scenes.visual: The two cell outlines recolour: the bacterium wall and membrane fill ORANGE, the archaeon wall and membrane fill CRIMSON, with a label 'different chemicals (schematic)'. The 'DNA' rung flashes briefly with a small gene-strip icon labelled 'genes differ (top rung)'. The cards slide apart into two boxes labelled 'Bacteria' and 'Archaea'.
scenes.narration: No. The chemicals that build their cell walls and membranes are different. Their genes, compared on the top rung, differ too. So scientists split them into two domains, Bacteria and Archaea.

scenes.tts: Every living thing whose cells have a nucleus goes in a third domain, Eukarya. So life has three domains. Kingdoms sit inside them. Fungi, plants and animals are kingdoms inside Eukarya. The paramecium waits. You will place it yourself.
scenes.visual: A large box labelled 'Eukarya' draws itself to the right of 'Bacteria' and 'Archaea'. Inside it, three smaller boxes form: 'Fungi' (mushroom), 'Plants' (oak), 'Animals' (deer). The paramecium card sits inside Eukarya but outside the three boxes, with a small '?' tag.
scenes.narration: Every living thing whose cells have a nucleus goes in a third domain, Eukarya. So life has three domains. Kingdoms sit inside them. Fungi, plants and animals are kingdoms inside Eukarya. The paramecium waits. You will place it yourself.

scenes.tts: Look back. The living things never changed. The evidence did, and new evidence could move a card to a new group.
scenes.visual: Quick rewind: the table replays the three layouts in a row, eyes, microscope, cell chemistry, as small thumbnails, with the mushroom card's path traced by a purple arrow from 'Plants' to 'Fungi'. Text on screen: 'same living things, new evidence'.
scenes.narration: Look back. The living things never changed. The evidence did, and new evidence could move a card to a new group.

scenes.tts: One rung is left, DNA. Scientists compare the same gene in different living things. Will the mushroom's gene match the oak's or the deer's more closely?
scenes.visual: 'DNA' rung lights at the top of the ladder. Two dotted lines run from the mushroom card, one toward the oak card and one toward the deer card, each ending in a '?'. No answer is shown.
scenes.narration: One rung is left, DNA. Scientists compare the same gene in different living things. Will the mushroom's gene match the oak's or the deer's more closely?

scenes.visual: End card with Hex mascot. Line: 'New evidence can move a living thing to a new group.'
